148.0.0.en: Alleluia. Praise the LORD from the heavens; praise Him in the heights. Praise Him, all His angels; praise Him, all His hosts.

148.0.2.en: 1- The writer of the psalm calls the heavens first to praise God. The heavens represent what is exalted above the earth and its inhabitants. And in the heavens is the throne of God, because of His great loftiness.

148.0.3.en: 2- The first group he calls to praise God is the angels, and God's hosts are the various ranks of angels.

148.0.4.en: He begins with the angels who praise in the heavens and in the heights, because their principal work is praise; they are the creatures most able to praise God, because they are spirits without bodies and they behold God at all times. Although the writer of the psalm knows that the angels praise God continually, he calls them to praise, since he is kindled with divine love and longs to praise; so the first group that came to his mind was the angels who praise at all times.

148.0.5.en: 3- To the extent that man lives a heavenly life he becomes like the angels, and he tastes a greater sweetness in praise, since he learns from the angels how praise should be, and he rises above material desires and acquires many spiritual virtues.

148.1.0.en: Praise Him, sun and moon; praise Him, all you stars of light. Praise Him, you heavens of heavens, and you waters that are above the heavens.

148.1.1.en: 1- After the writer of the psalm has called the angels to praise God, who represent the first group of those who praise, that is, the first choir, he calls the second group, that is, the second choir in praise, which is the heavenly bodies; so he calls the sun and the moon and the stars of light. He also calls the heaven of heavens, and we understand from this that there are a number of heavens, all of which he calls to praise God. What is known to us is three heavens: the heaven of the birds, then the heaven of cosmic space, that is, the heavenly bodies, and after that the heaven of the angels, which is called the third heaven to which Paul was caught up. He also calls the waters above the heavens, which are those that evaporated from the earth and rose to the sky, and then return and fall upon the earth as rain. The praise of God by these beings is by the course of these stars in the order that God has set for them. Likewise man glorifies God not only by his words but also by his deeds. The heavens also do works that benefit man, such as giving light and rain. All these are works that praise God.

148.1.2.en: 2- The heavens are a type of the spiritual man who by his good conduct gives light to those around him, like the sun, the moon and the stars, and who pours out love and services on others like the rain; all these are praises offered to God through the works of spiritual people.

148.2.0.en: Let them praise the name of the LORD: for He commanded, and they were created. He has also established them for ever and ever: He has made a decree which shall not pass.

148.2.1.en: God rejoices in His creation that praises Him, and it praises Him for three things:

148.2.2.en: 1- "For He commanded, and they were created": because He created the heavens by His command and His word. We now try, through studies and research, to understand something about them and their order, yet all this came about at once by the command of God.

148.2.3.en: In the same way God also commands, and gives man the gifts of the Holy Spirit to meet the needs of the Church, such as preaching and teaching, and the fruits of the Holy Spirit, that is, the virtues for the building up of the spiritual man.

148.2.4.en: 2- "He has established them for ever": God set for them a fixed order in which they move, continuing throughout all of life.

148.2.5.en: In the same way God also set an order of worship in the Church, called the rites, to help man in his relationship with God. And when the spiritual man is steadfast in the Church, God helps him, so that he is established forever in His heavenly Kingdom.

148.2.6.en: 3- "He has made a decree which shall not pass": God was not content to set an order for them, but also set limits which they do not exceed, so that the stars do not collide with one another and bring catastrophes upon the universe. He also placed the sun at a distance from the earth that does not burn human beings. And God likewise sets limits for human beings so that they do not wrong others beyond measure, and He permits some weakness so that man does not go further in his evil.

148.2.7.en: The heavens and what is in them represent the presence of God, and their submission to Him calls you, my brother, to live by the commandments of God and to be faithful in your works, and so to glorify God and praise Him like His heavenly creatures.

148.3.0.en: Praise the LORD from the earth, you dragons and all deeps.

148.3.1.en: 1- The writer of the psalm moves to a new group, a third group that praises God, which is the earth and what is on it, and likewise the seas and what is in them. In this verse he mentions the dragons, plural of dragon, a huge and powerful animal that lives either on the land, like the huge serpent, or in the deeps, which are the depths of the waters, or on their shores, like whales and crocodiles. He chose these predatory and huge animals to declare that all animals, even the predatory among them, praise God by following the order that God has set.

148.3.2.en: 2- The dragons represent huge and predatory animals and are a type of anger. When man sees these dragons moving in their order, whatever his strength or position, he submits to God, controls his anger, and strives for prayer, praise and love for others. The deeps are also a type of the depths, so man should praise God in his depths, that is, with all his feelings.

148.4.0.en: Fire and hail; snow and vapours; stormy wind fulfilling His word.

148.4.1.en: 1- He mentions a group of natural phenomena that affect the earth, such as fire, hail, snow, vapours and stormy wind; all of these move in the order that God has set for them, and do not depart from their nature except by the command of God, like the fire that did not harm the three youths.

148.4.2.en: 2- These natural phenomena represent the trials in man's life, and when God permits these trials it is for man's good, since all things work together for good to those who love God. And when man accepts them and continues in his prayers and praise, God gives him many blessings because of his endurance. All the more so since all these phenomena fulfil the word of God, that is, they carry out His commands, and they are all for the benefit of man, who does not understand their meaning at first glance, but by submitting to the will of God he understands with time the purpose of God and receives His blessing.

148.5.0.en: Mountains and all hills; fruitful trees and all cedars.

148.5.1.en: 1- The mountains and the hills, that is, the very high places and those of medium height, praise God. They represent the steadfastness and strength that man imitates in his relationship with God, and likewise loftiness and nearness to God. God ordained the existence of these mountains and hills to glorify Him by their steadfastness, so that man may imitate them and learn from them.

148.5.2.en: 2- The fruitful trees, or the unfruitful ones such as the cedar, all glorify God, and every tree has its use. The wood of the cedar tree is very precious, so that man may know that he can glorify God by using his abilities, and not compare himself with others, but do his duty faithfully; and God rejoices in man's work as a glorification of Him.

148.6.0.en: Beasts and all cattle; creeping things and flying fowl.

148.6.1.en: 1- The beasts, which are the predatory animals, glorify God in their conduct by the particular instincts and natures that God has given them. The spiritual man should control and direct his instincts for the glory of God: he is angry with himself so as to repent, and he is strong and quick to rescue the imprisoned; that is, he uses his strong abilities for the glory of God. This is the praise that God asks for.

148.6.2.en: 2- And all cattle, creeping things: this means all the tame animals that move upon the earth, which are useful to man in one way or another. In the same way man learns to serve others as much as he can, and so glorifies God.

148.6.3.en: 3- Flying fowl: birds are a type of loftiness and rising toward heaven, and so they are a type of leaving earthly desires; and whenever man tries to rise in prayer to heaven and to control his desires, God is glorified in him.

148.6.4.en: Contemplate, my brother, the creatures around you on the earth, that you may learn from their conduct something for your benefit, and so rejoice the heart of God, and thank Him and praise Him.

148.7.0.en: Kings of the earth and all peoples; princes and all judges of the earth; both young men and maidens; old men and children: let them praise the name of the LORD, for His name alone is excellent; His glory is above the earth and heaven.

148.7.1.en: 1- If the psalm spoke first of the angels who praise God at all times in the heavens, it concludes the psalm by speaking of the praise of human beings, who ought to be like the angels in praise, even if their bodies hinder them in part, but their goal, which ought always to be before them, is the praise of God.

148.7.2.en: 2- If the inanimate creation mentioned in (vv. 7-10) praises God by submitting to the order on which God created it, man rises above it, since he has a mind and a choice, and his love for God appears when he praises Him and does not cling to the passing material things of the earth.

148.7.3.en: 3- The psalm calls all classes of the people to praise God, whether kings, or princes, or judges, and on the other side those who are ruled, or governed, who are under the leadership of those previously mentioned; all give thanks to God for what He has ordained and given to them. For the peoples everywhere praise God, who has organized for them states, rulers, kings and judges who govern their lives by ordered laws.

148.7.4.en: Likewise everyone who holds a place of leadership praises God for the grace of leadership and authority.

148.7.5.en: 4- The psalm also calls the people in their different ages: the young, male and female, who ought to praise God first because they are full of vitality and energy; and likewise the old men with experience with God, and the boys who have not reached youth but who perceive the greatness of God, so that they praise with the young and the old; for man ought to praise God in all the stages of his life, because in every stage he enjoys God's care.

148.7.6.en: 5- God alone deserves praise from all human beings, because He is higher than everything that is called god, and above everything in heaven and on earth, because He is the Creator and Governor of them all. All the great creatures declare that their Creator is, of course, greater than they.

148.8.0.en: He also exalts the horn of His people, the praise of all His saints; even of the children of Israel, a people near to Him. Alleluia. Exalts: raises up.

148.8.1.en: 1- The psalm concludes with a call to the people of God to praise Him, for the following reasons:

148.8.2.en: a- He gives them great power that distinguishes them from the rest of the peoples, which is symbolized by the horn that appears on an animal when it matures. For God gives His people strength among all peoples, as He protects them and defends them, and by His power they even defeat their enemies the demons.

148.8.3.en: b- God gives them a glory in which they boast and for which they thank God. So He is glorified in their words and deeds. And He gives glory especially to His people because they are godly, that is, they fear Him, so they live in repentance and keep away from evil, and so enjoy purity.

148.8.4.en: c- God grants them the grace of drawing near to Him, so that they enjoy not only His protection and His support for them throughout their lives, but beyond this they delight in fellowship with Him and rejoice not only on earth, but He takes them with Him to heaven, to rejoice with Him forever in His Kingdom.

148.8.5.en: 2- The power, the glory and the close fellowship with God appeared clearly in the Incarnation of Christ and the graces of the Holy Spirit in the Church, which are made complete for the children of God in eternal life.

148.8.6.en: 3- The whole psalm ends with the word Alleluia, that is, a call to all creatures to exult before God, and rejoice and praise Him, because praise fills the heart with joy.

148.8.7.en: Contemplate the blessings of God which He has given you in the New Testament in His Church, and in your personal life, so that they may move your heart and urge you to praise Him, not only in the Church with the rest of the faithful, but also in your inner room; and after this it extends to be with you in all your steps, that is, you live a life of praise continually.

148.8.8.en: The praise of the people of God "Alleluia. Sing to the LORD a new song, and His praise in the congregation of saints" v. 1 Introduction:

148.8.9.en: 1- Its writer: unknown, since the psalm has no title or mention of the writer; it is one of the orphan psalms whose writer is unknown.

148.8.10.en: 2- When was it written? There are two opinions about the time of its writing:

148.8.11.en: a- The days of the Maccabees, since it mentions victory over the resisting peoples.

148.8.12.en: b- After the return from captivity, when the people of God lived in safety after the resistance of the wicked had subsided.

148.8.13.en: 3- This psalm is one of the psalms of praise which call the people of God to praise Him for their salvation and the subjection of the enemies to them; and it is to be noted that it begins and ends with the word Alleluia. It is one of the five Hallel psalms (Ps 146-150).

148.8.14.en: 4- This psalm is suitable for every believer who wants to rejoice in praising God and to strengthen his faith in the power of God that supports him.

148.8.15.en: 5- This psalm is a prophecy about Christ the Savior of the Church, and about victory over the demons by the Cross.

148.8.16.en: 6- This psalm is prayed in the Church daily in the Midnight Praise (Tasbeha), as it is part of the Fourth Hoos with which the day's Midnight Praise begins.

148.8.17.en: 7- This psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.

149.0.0.en: Alleluia. Sing to the LORD a new song, and His praise in the congregation of saints.

149.0.1.en: 1- The psalm calls the godly people of God, that is, those who fear Him, keep away from evil, and are reverent before Him in prayers, to praise Him with a new song. The meaning is that whoever is accustomed to singing grows in the knowledge of God and in praising Him, and so offers every day songs with a new feeling, deeper according to his perception of the fear of God and his beholding of His love.

149.0.2.en: 2- This verse is a prophecy of the singing to Christ the Savior, to whom we sing a new song, and in it we feel the fulfilment of the type in Him and we see the carrying out of His promises, so our hearts rejoice and we fear Him because of the greatness of His salvation, and we sing the new song, especially after we have tasted the new birth in Baptism and our hearts have been attached to our eternal inheritance, so we sing a song deeper than the usual songs.

149.1.0.en: Let Israel rejoice in Him that made him; let the children of Zion be joyful in their King.

149.1.1.en: 1- The psalm calls the people of God, Israel, to rejoice in God who created them out of nothing, and to sing to Him because He made them a people of His own, so He became their King and their God, who shepherds them, keeps them, defends them, and provides for their needs continually.

149.1.2.en: 2- This verse is also a prophecy about Christ, who gives those who believe in Him the grace of the new creation by the second birth in Baptism, and they rejoice in Christ their King, who reigns over their hearts. And the more their hearts are attached to His love, the more they long that He reign over them forever in the Kingdom of Heaven.

149.2.0.en: Let them praise His name in the dance; let them sing praises to Him with the timbrel and harp.

149.2.1.en: 1- Although pagan worship involved worship with dancing and musical instruments, the psalm moves the people of God to worship Him with reverence through devotional dance, like the dance of the women behind Miriam the sister of Moses at the going out from the Red Sea (Ex 15:20), and like the dance of David before the ark of the covenant of God when it was brought to Jerusalem (2 Sam 6:14). The intention is to express joy by the movement of the body and by musical instruments, in addition to the tongue and all the feelings of the heart. And this devotional dance that took place in the Old Testament is entirely different from the dance of debauchery and of the passions which Satan stirs up to draw people away from God; whether in ancient times, as the children of Israel did before the golden calf which Aaron made, and which Moses destroyed (Ex 32:19, 20), or the dancing in our contemporary days which takes place in places of amusement and to satisfy the passions, and which draws man away from God, since it has no reverence or fear of God.

149.2.2.en: 2- In the Septuagint and Coptic translation we find the beginning of this verse as "Let them praise His holy name in rows (in a choir)." The rows are the plural of a row, that is, in an order of rows and choirs for offering ordered songs to God, and the word dance is not mentioned.

149.3.0.en: For the LORD takes pleasure in His people; He will beautify the meek with salvation.

149.3.1.en: 1- What moves the people of God to praise Him is that God is pleased with them. For God in His humility cares for His people, and rejoices and is pleased with His people who love Him and praise Him, so He blesses them, and even gives them His salvation, because they are meek and humble before Him, so He saves them from their enemies and keeps them from all evil; for meekness is a condition for receiving salvation. The human part is striving to walk in humility and meekness, and the divine part, that is, the work of grace, is that God gives them salvation.

149.3.2.en: 2- The divine pleasure became clear by faith in Christ, and the believers' receiving of salvation, which begins in the Sacrament of Baptism, as those baptized come forward with meekness, humility and repentance if they are adults, and so receive the new birth and become members in the Body of Christ, that is, the Church.

149.4.0.en: Let the saints be joyful in glory; let them sing aloud upon their beds.

149.4.1.en: Their beds: plural of bed, which is the couch.

149.4.2.en: 1- Those who fear God live in purity and keep away from sin, and their hearts rejoice, and they behold the glory of God and rejoice in fellowship with Him, and this joy appears in praising God throughout the day, then in the inner room, and even after lying down on the bed, man continues to praise until he is absorbed in sleep. By this he keeps away from every evil thought, or negligence and laziness.

149.4.3.en: 2- God is glorified in the godly by their words and deeds, who keep their purity even in their inner rooms and on their beds; and until the end of their lives when they lie down finally in death, and their spirits rise to continue praising God in heaven.

149.4.4.en: Look at God's gifts and His new works with you, so that you may sing to Him with a new spirit, and enjoy a deeper enjoyment of fellowship with Him.

149.5.0.en: Let the high praises of God be in their mouth, and a twoedged sword in their hand.

149.5.1.en: High praises: plural of an extolling, which is commendation and exaltation; in the Septuagint it is "exaltations", which gives the same meaning.

149.5.2.en: 1- Since the faithful have become accustomed to praise throughout the day, and even when they lie down on their beds, the praise and exaltation of God has become continually in their mouths, being their chief concern in thought, heart and tongue.

149.5.3.en: 2- Besides praise, God gives them power which is expressed by the twoedged sword, which strikes right and left to lay low the enemies, the demons; that is, God gives them power to triumph over the enemies. The sword is also a type of the powerful word of God, which frightens and lays low the demons.

149.5.4.en: 3- This verse applies to Christ, who glorified the Father, and whose word was like a twoedged sword that lays low the demons and delivers the children of men from them.

149.6.0.en: To execute vengeance upon the heathen, and punishments upon the people; to bind their kings with chains, and their nobles with fetters of iron.

149.6.2.en: 1- God gives His children power to take vengeance on Satan and to chastise the wicked who followed the devil and went away from God. The faithful are an instrument by which God chastises the wicked so that they return to Him, and they bind their kings, the demons, and their nobles, the wicked who follow the demons, and so prevent them by the power of the Cross from harming the righteous.

149.6.3.en: 2- Although the victory was accomplished for the people of God over the pagan peoples whom God commanded to be destroyed in Canaan in the days of Joshua, and in the age of the Judges, then the days of David, and extended throughout the Old Testament until the days of the Maccabees, it appeared more in the victory over the wars of the demons in the New Testament, as in the temptation of Christ on the mountain, and in the lives of the saints throughout the generations until now.

149.6.4.en: 3- The binding and chastisement of the wicked and their leaders was accomplished with the heretics, whom the ecumenical councils cut off, and before whom the Church stood throughout the generations, and until now.

149.7.0.en: To execute upon them the judgment written: this honour have all His saints. Alleluia.

149.7.1.en: 1- The children of God, by chastising the wicked and triumphing over them, carry out and execute the judgment of God issued against the wicked, which He declared in the Holy Bible (Isa 10:1; Rom 6:23). Indeed the whole Holy Bible declares God's rejection of sin, whether in the pagans who refuse to worship God, or the heretics who disturb the faith.

149.7.2.en: 2- When God chastises the wicked He restores to His godly ones their honour, for the wicked have wronged them much, but in the end the godly must be honoured and chastised, then He takes vengeance on the wicked. This shows the justice of God, so He establishes the righteous in a life of righteousness.

149.7.3.en: 3- The psalm ends with the word Alleluia as it began with it, that is, the godly of God exult in their praises to Him, and in their thanks to God who takes vengeance on the wicked and honours His children.

149.7.4.en: Do not be disturbed by the temporary success of the wicked, by which they deceive themselves, and do not be deceived like them, but hold fast to the commandments of God and His fear, and you will live reassured, and indeed in great joy.

149.7.5.en: Praise is the joy of the saints "Alleluia. Praise God in His sanctuary; praise Him in the firmament of His power" v. 1 Introduction:

149.7.6.en: 1- Its writer: unknown, since the psalm has no title and no mention of the writer; it is one of the orphan psalms whose writer is unknown.

149.7.7.en: 2- This psalm is the conclusion of the Hallel psalms (Ps 146-150). This psalm is distinguished by praising God out of love for Him, and not for a petition, or thanksgiving, or confession.

149.7.8.en: 3- This psalm is a prophetic psalm, which prophesies about praise in the New Testament, and also praise in the Kingdom of Heaven.

149.7.9.en: 4- This psalm is liturgical, as it is the last part of the Fourth Hoos, which is prayed at the beginning of the day's Midnight Praise. It is also said at the end of the Divine Liturgy at the distribution of the Mysteries.

149.7.10.en: 5- This psalm calls for the use of all the musical instruments to praise God, and they are a type of all of man's abilities, that is, man praises God with his whole being as much as he can on earth, and then in perfection in the heavens.

149.7.11.en: 6- This psalm is not found in the prayers of the Agpeya.
